Philadelphia County by the numbers

Which city offices run property tax for the county?

The City of Philadelphia handles it all. The county has had the same borders as the city since the consolidation of 1854, and the county offices were folded into city government in 1952, so there is no separate county tax bill or county treasurer to call.

Three city bodies share the work. The Office of Property Assessment sets the value of every parcel. The Department of Revenue bills and collects the Real Estate Tax. The Board of Revision of Taxes hears formal appeals of those values. The county covers 143 square miles, of which 134 are land, and it is the only first class county in Pennsylvania.

Philadelphia County is also one of the three counties William Penn laid out in 1682, together with Bucks and Chester. Today it borders Bucks, Montgomery and Delaware counties in Pennsylvania and Burlington, Camden and Gloucester counties across the river in New Jersey. The Census Bureau estimated the county population at 1,574,281 in July 2025.

How is a house in Philadelphia County assessed?

The Office of Property Assessment values a house using its size, age, location and condition, along with recent sales of comparable homes nearby. It draws on field inspections, aerial photos, permit and deed data from other city departments, and listing and sales data.

For tax year 2027 the City mailed new Notices of Valuation in late June 2026, covering more than 580,000 properties. The City's own estimate was a bill change of about $97 for the median-valued home, though any single house can land well above or below that. A notice is not a bill, and an owner who gets none usually had no change in market value, or has an outdated mailing address on file with the office.

The new values start with the tax year itself. Bills for that year go out the December before and fall due on March 31.

What is the Philadelphia County property tax rate and when is it due?

For tax year 2025 the City published a total rate of 1.3998 percent of assessed value: 0.6159 percent for the City and 0.7839 percent for the school district. The bill is due March 31 each year.

Paying late adds charges at 1.5 percent a month starting April 1. If the tax is still unpaid on January 1 of the next year, up to a 15 percent addition goes on, the account is registered delinquent, a lien is filed for the total, and the City may begin the sheriff sale process. Revenue's foreclosure warning letter adds that further interest and fees land on January 1 and February 1 once the account turns delinquent.

Owners can settle a bill on the Philadelphia Tax Center, over the phone, by check to a Philadelphia post office box, or at the Municipal Services Building and the North and Northeast Philadelphia satellite offices. Ask the Department of Revenue for the current box number and office hours before you go.

How can an owner contest a county assessment?

Start with a First Level Review at the Office of Property Assessment, then, or instead, file a formal appeal with the Board of Revision of Taxes. Formal appeals are due the first Monday in October ahead of the tax year they affect, so a 2028 value is challenged in October 2027. The table shows how the 2027 cycle ran.

Tax year 2027 assessment calendar, City of Philadelphia
DateEvent
June 29, 2026Notices of Valuation mailed and values posted online
September 1, 2026First Level Review deadline (closed)
October 5, 2026Board of Revision of Taxes filing deadline (closed)
December 1, 2026Revenue begins mailing tax bills
January 1, 2027New assessments take effect
March 31, 2027Payment due

Source: City of Philadelphia announcement on 2027 assessments.

The Board accepts appeals that show the market value is too high or too low, that the value is not uniform with similar nearby homes, or that the recorded characteristics of the property are substantially wrong. Filing is by mail, email or in person at 601 Walnut Street, Suite 325 East, and hearings can be held in person or by video. Notice of the hearing arrives about 45 to 90 days ahead. Two late-filing exceptions help buyers: a new owner who takes a deed between the first Monday of October and December 31 has 30 days from the deed, and a buyer who signs an agreement of sale in that window has 30 days from signing.

Which relief programs can lower a Philadelphia County bill?

Resident owners have the most choices here, and most of them shrink the balance well before a sale becomes a risk.

  • Homestead Exemption: cuts the taxable part of an owner-occupied home's assessment by $100,000 in 2027, up from $80,000 for 2023 bills.
  • Installment plan: lets seniors and income-qualified owners pay the current year in monthly installments rather than one March payment.
  • Tax freeze: senior and low-income versions keep the bill from rising with later rate or assessment increases.
  • Longtime Owner Occupants Program: caps the taxable value for owners of ten or more years who face a steep assessment jump.
  • Owner-occupied payment agreement: sets monthly payments on past-due tax from household income and size.
  • Disabled veterans exemption and a catastrophic loss adjustment for damage that cuts value by 50 percent or more.

Pennsylvania also runs a Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and adults with disabilities, with a Philadelphia district office that takes questions.

How does a sale settle the tax on a Philadelphia County house?

The seller owes the tax through the closing date, and any past-due balance comes out of the seller's share at the settlement table. A lien does not vanish on a sale, so title companies search for property tax, water and sewer liens first.

  • Water liens are searchable at water-lien.phila.gov, and a payoff request goes to the Water Department by email a month ahead of settlement.
  • The 4.578 percent Realty Transfer Tax, which is 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the Commonwealth, is paid at recording and is usually split between buyer and seller.
  • An unpaid water lien passes to the new owner, which is why the payoff is requested before the sale.

An owner facing a short timeline can request a cash offer on the property in its current condition, with the title company paying the City from the seller's side.

How does Philadelphia County housing look in the Census survey?

  • Census survey respondents put a typical owned home at $243,100 for 2020 through 2024.
  • About 51.8 percent of households own the place they live in, so nearly half rent.
  • Gross rent has a middle of $1,397, and the middle household income is $61,953.
  • The county counted 764,829 housing units in 2025.

Those figures are countywide, so a rowhouse in one neighborhood can sit far from the middle.

More questions about Philadelphia County, PA Property Tax Guide

Does Philadelphia County have a separate county tax bill?

No. The city and county are the same territory, and the Department of Revenue sends one Real Estate Tax bill that covers the City and the School District of Philadelphia. Ask that department for the balance on any parcel.

When is the Philadelphia County property tax due?

March 31 of each year. Bills are usually mailed in December, and monthly additions of one and a half percent begin April 1 on any open balance.

When must a formal assessment appeal be filed?

Early October of the year before the tax year, specifically the first Monday. For tax year 2027 the date was October 5, 2026, and exceptions of 30 days apply to people who bought or signed an agreement of sale late in the year.

Can the City sell my house for unpaid tax?

Yes. Unpaid tax becomes a lien after January 1 of the following year, and the City can then start the sheriff sale process. Owners who live in the home can ask for an owner-occupied payment agreement first.

Who pays the tax when I sell?

The seller pays through the closing date, and the title company clears any lien. Ask the Department of Revenue for the tax balance and the Water Department for the water payoff well before settlement.

Allegheny County by the numbers

Who sets and who collects property tax in Allegheny County, PA?

Two county offices split the work, and neither one sets the full bill. The Office of Property Assessments decides what each parcel is worth for tax purposes, and the Treasurer's Office prepares and collects the county's share of the tax.

Your school district and municipality set their own millage rates and send separate bills, which the Treasurer's page makes clear: that office only collects Allegheny County real estate tax. The county rate was raised to 6.43 mills in 2025, meaning $6.43 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value.

In 2025 the Treasurer's Office collected more than $500 million across more than 550,000 parcels, which the office says is about 45% of the county's operating budget.

How are Allegheny County properties assessed?

Allegheny County uses base year assessments, and the base year is 2012, with a value date of January 1, 2012. The last countywide reassessment took effect for tax year 2013, and the county has used the same base year since.

That means a house gets a new assessed value only for narrow reasons:

  • An omission or a mathematical or clerical error.
  • A physical change, such as a demolition, a subdivision or work under a building permit.
  • An interim assessment that a school district or municipality asks for on new construction or major improvements.
  • A catastrophic loss, which requires an application within six months of the loss.

The assessed values on the county's Real Estate parcel search show the base year value of a property, with the changes above, and they do not track current sale prices. A sale, even a very high one, does not change the assessment by itself.

When are Allegheny County property taxes due?

County tax bills go out in January, and the cheapest day to pay is on or before March 31. The calendar below comes from the Treasurer's office.

Allegheny County real estate tax calendar, Treasurer's Office
DateWhat happens
JanuaryAssessments are certified and tax statements are mailed
March 31Last day for the 2% discount off the gross tax
April 30Last day to pay the gross (face) amount
May 1Past due period starts: a one-time 5% penalty plus 1% interest a month
June 30Annual deadline to apply for Senior Citizen Tax Relief

The Treasurer's Office handles only the current tax year. Taxes still unpaid go to Jordan Tax Service on January 1 of each year, and the office directs owners with delinquent or liened years to Jordan Tax Service at 412-835-5243. Continued nonpayment can end in a Sheriff Sale of the property.

The calendar above is a recurring schedule, so check the date printed on your own bill each year.

How do I appeal an Allegheny County assessment?

File with the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review, known as BPAAR, which is the first level of appeal. The annual appeal window for the 2027 tax year ran from July 1 through September 1, 2026, and the window closed on that date.

BPAAR runs the process itself, including scheduling, hearing notices and postponements. All hearings are held by telephone. Residential hearing notices are mailed at least 14 days ahead, and commercial notices at least 21 days ahead. The county has published 49.3% as the common level ratio for the 2027 tax year, applied to market value in appeals heard starting in September 2026.

  • An owner may appear alone, hire an attorney, or name an authorized representative.
  • A school district, a municipality or the county can file an appeal on the same parcel; the owner may attend but does not have to.
  • Only the party who filed can withdraw an appeal.
  • A losing party can take the BPAAR decision to the Court of Common Pleas, through the Board of Viewers.

A Special Appeal can be filed year round, but only in response to a written determination notice from the Office of Property Assessments.

Which tax relief programs exist in Allegheny County?

The county lists several programs that can lower a bill. Two matter most to homeowners.

  • Act 50, the Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion, cuts a primary residence's assessed value by $18,000 for county tax purposes only.
  • Act 77, Senior Citizen Tax Relief, gives a 30% reduction in the county bill to owners who are at least 60, earn $30,000 or less a year, and have lived in and owned the home for at least 10 years. The Treasurer's deadline to apply is June 30.

Other programs include Act 76 (LERTA) abatements for commercial and industrial property in some municipalities, Act 156 Clean and Green for land in farm or forest use, a Residential Visitability Design Tax Credit under Act 132, and a catastrophic loss reduction for structures that lost 50% or more of their value to fire or a natural disaster. A Volunteer Service Tax Credit rewards eligible emergency responders.

Act 50 covers primary residences only, so a house that turns into a rental falls outside it. A seller who sells to a landlord should expect the new owner's bill to lose that $18,000 reduction.

What happens to tax when I sell a house in Allegheny County?

The Treasurer's real estate tax department prepares delinquent tax files and property liens, and it also manages tax certification requests, which is where a closing agent can ask about a parcel's county tax status before the sale.

Property tax is separate from the transfer tax at recording, which runs from 2% to 5% in the county depending on the municipality and school district. For the county's own examples, a $40,000 house costs $800 in transfer tax in Shaler Township and $2,000 in the City of Pittsburgh.

A new rule also affects investors who buy rentals. Effective September 18, 2026, Act 29 of 2026 requires buyers of non-owner-occupied real estate to give contact details to the county's chief assessor within 30 days of purchase. Corporate and LLC owners must name an individual who is authorized to fix code violations, and owners have 30 days to report any change. Failure to comply, or knowingly giving false information, can bring a fine of up to $500.

What does Allegheny County look like on paper?

Allegheny County spans 745 square miles at the point where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers form the Ohio. It contains 130 municipalities, which is why local millage and transfer tax rates differ so widely, and it is Pennsylvania's second most populous county.

Allegheny County snapshot, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureFigure
Population, July 2025 estimate1,225,035
Housing units614,484
Owner-occupied housing rate65.2%
Median owner-occupied value$227,600
Median selected owner cost with a mortgage$1,685 a month
Median selected owner cost without a mortgage$654 a month

Monthly owner costs without a mortgage, $654, give a sense of the carrying cost for an owner who pays a county bill, a school bill and a municipal bill on a house with no loan.

More questions about Allegheny County, PA Property Tax Guide

Is there a discount for paying Allegheny County property tax early?

Yes. The county gives a 2% discount off the gross tax on payments made by March 31, and the face amount is due through April 30.

What penalty applies after April 30 in Allegheny County?

Starting May 1 an unpaid bill picks up a one-time 5% penalty, and then 1% interest on the gross tax for every month it stays unpaid. Past years move to Jordan Tax Service on January 1.

When did the most recent Allegheny County appeal window close?

The 2027 tax year window opened July 1, 2026 and closed September 1, 2026. File through BPAAR; a later filing waits for the next annual season.

Does Allegheny County reassess a house when it sells?

No. Assessments rest on a 2012 base year, and the county changes a value only for omissions, errors, physical changes, interim requests or catastrophic loss.

Who runs the senior discount in Allegheny County?

The Treasurer's Office administers Senior Citizen Tax Relief. Applicants must be 60 or older, earn $30,000 or less, and have owned and lived in the home 10 years, with a June 30 yearly deadline.

Montgomery County by the numbers

Which Montgomery County offices deal with property tax?

Two county offices matter to a seller: the Board of Assessment Appeals, which sets values, and the Tax Claim Bureau, which pursues delinquent bills. Both sit in Norristown, the county seat.

The Board of Assessment Appeals values and assesses all real estate for county, municipal and school tax purposes. It also keeps the assessment rolls, the tax maps and the registry of who owns each parcel. The office phone is 610-278-3761. Walk-in filings are taken in Norristown on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:00, and the registry window shuts a little sooner, at 3:45.

Anyone dividing a lot before a sale has a third contact. Lot line changes and requests for a new parcel number go to the Board's Mapping Division, reached through the same phone number or at boamapping@montgomerycountypa.gov.

The county, the municipality and the school district all draw on that one assessed value. For the current bill from the municipal or school side, ask the municipality or the school district, since the Board sets values rather than collecting the tax.

When is the Montgomery County assessment appeal deadline?

Annual appeals are due by August 1, and the county applies that same date to applications for real estate tax exemption. A published county notice explains the reason: state law requires all annual appeals to be heard and acted on by October 31, and changes must reach the rolls and the owner and taxing districts by November 15, citing Title 53 Pa.C.S. section 8844.

The Board's forms page lists the documents an owner is likely to need.

  • Assessment appeal form and a separate commercial appeal procedure.
  • Assessment appeal fees schedule, which the county publishes as its own document.
  • Homestead application, homestead appeal form and homestead removal form.
  • Exemption application and instructions.
  • Appeal rules and regulations, and a notice for appeals pending in court.
  • Mailing address change form and a list of taxing authorities.
  • A Taxpayer Relief Act document and a notice on an assessor's right to enter a property.

The Board also warns about postmarks. Delays in the mail can cause a timely filing to be stamped late, so the county suggests asking for a hand-cancelled postmark, a certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or postage bought at the counter. Hand delivery to the Norristown office avoids the issue.

How does the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau sell tax-delinquent property?

The Bureau can sell a parcel four ways under the Real Estate Tax Sale law: upset sale, private sale, judicial sale and repository sale. A property that has gone unsold moves along that sequence, and the buyer's liability changes at each step.

  • Upset sale: scheduled each September and December for parcels whose taxes from two years earlier are still unpaid. Buyers take the property subject to all liens.
  • Private sale: possible after a parcel has been exposed but not sold. A written bid goes to the Bureau, and anyone objecting has 45 days to petition the court.
  • Judicial sale: held at least once each year in August and December, only for exposed parcels that did not sell. Parcels are presented free and clear of liens.
  • Repository sale: for properties unsold at judicial sale, with each taxing district reviewing any bid.
Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau sale schedule listed for 2026
SaleDate on the county page
Judicial saleAugust 20, 2026
Upset saleSeptember 24, 2026
Continued judicial saleDecember 10, 2026
Continued upset saleDecember 10, 2026

Source: Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau. Sales are advertised in two newspapers and the Montgomery Bar Association journal within two months of the sale.

Regular mail to the Bureau goes to P.O. Box 190, Norristown, PA 19404, and overnight carriers use One Montgomery Plaza, Suite 600. Its desk is staffed on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:15. Ask the Bureau for the schedule beyond 2026.

Does a Montgomery County seller owe transfer tax at closing?

Usually, unless the transfer is exempt. The commonwealth taxes the value of the property at 1 percent, and the grantor and grantee both answer for it. The county recorder takes payment as the deed is lodged and sends the state share on, while local rates come from the municipality and school district.

Exempt transfers include certain gifts within a family, deeds to government units and estates that pass at death. Because municipalities set their own local share, the closing agent should confirm the combined rate for the specific property address rather than assume a county-wide figure.

Real estate taxes themselves are usually prorated at closing between buyer and seller according to the sales contract. Any amount already delinquent is a separate matter, because the Tax Claim Bureau pursues those balances and the closing agent will want them settled.

What does Montgomery County look like for a seller preparing to list?

Montgomery County borders Philadelphia on its southeast side and was created on September 10, 1784 from part of Philadelphia County. It covers 487 square miles, and its 856,553 residents in the 2020 census make it the third most populous county in Pennsylvania. There were 346,877 housing units, with 70.8 percent of occupied homes owner-occupied and 29.2 percent rented.

The county has 22 operating school districts, including Abington, Boyertown Area, Cheltenham, Colonial, Hatboro-Horsham, Jenkintown, Lower Merion, Methacton, Norristown Area, North Penn, Pottstown, Souderton Area, Upper Merion Area, Wissahickon and Spring-Ford Area, plus Bryn Athyn, which exists as an entity but runs no schools. The district that serves a house affects its tax bill and often how buyers weigh it, so a listing should name it.

Employment is spread across business parks in Blue Bell, Lansdale, Fort Washington, Horsham and King of Prussia, and many residents commute into Philadelphia.

How should a Montgomery County owner handle a house with unpaid tax?

Start with the bill. Find out which taxing body is owed, since county, municipal and school balances are separate, and ask the Tax Claim Bureau whether the parcel has been returned to it. A parcel that has reached the Bureau can end up at an upset sale once the taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid.

If a sale is scheduled for the parcel, ask the Bureau what must be paid to take it off the list. The Board's forms page also lists homestead and exemption applications, so ask the Board whether the property qualifies and file by the August 1 date.

A seller with a time problem can also sell the house before the Bureau does. That route keeps the deed in the seller's hands and lets the closing pay the tax from the proceeds.

More questions about Montgomery County, PA Property Tax Guide

What is the deadline for a Montgomery County assessment appeal?

August 1 is the annual filing deadline, and the county applies it to tax exemption applications too. Hearings are to be finished by October 31, and results must reach owners and taxing districts by November 15.

Where is the Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals?

In Norristown. Mail goes to P.O. Box 311, Norristown, PA 19404-0311, the phone is 610-278-3761, and in-person filings are accepted from 8:30 to 4:00 on weekdays.

Does Montgomery County sell homes for unpaid taxes?

Yes. The Tax Claim Bureau sells delinquent parcels at upset, private, judicial and repository sales. Upset sales are held each September and December, and judicial sales at least once a year in August and December.

Do buyers at a Montgomery County upset sale take on liens?

Yes, at upset and private sales, where the Bureau says the buyer assumes responsibility for all liens. Parcels at a judicial sale are offered free and clear of liens.

Can I mail a Montgomery County appeal on August 1?

Only with proof of the mailing date. The Board advises a hand-cancelled postmark, certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or counter-purchased postage, and it also accepts hand delivery in Norristown.

Bucks County by the numbers

Who sends a property tax bill in Bucks County?

Three bodies tax a Bucks County house: the township or borough, the school district and the county. The county's Tax Claim Bureau explains that each tax is the assessed value multiplied by that year's millage rate, so one parcel can carry three separate levies. County and township bills go out in early March, and school district bills follow in early July.

A change in assessment, such as new construction, produces an interim bill. Interim bills arrive quarterly and are added to the two annual bills. Each municipality has its own elected tax collector, and the county keeps a directory of them online.

Assessed value comes from a separate office. The Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals has three members, sets the market value of every parcel and calculates the assessment. Its staff prepares the tax rolls, maintains the tax maps, assigns parcel numbers and labels each document headed for recording. It does not set millage, which the taxing bodies decide.

What is it like to sell a house in Bucks County?

Bucks County is a large, mostly suburban county on the Delaware River, and prices sit well above the state's rural counties. It covers 622 square miles, with Doylestown as the seat, and its southern third, known as Lower Bucks, is flat coastal plain near Philadelphia and Trenton. Upper Bucks is hillier farmland and village country.

William Penn created the county in 1682. Housing grew in waves: the Levittown development of the 1950s added about 17,000 homes, and building later moved north into Middletown, Lower Makefield, Northampton and Newtown. Today the biggest townships by 2020 population are Bensalem, Bristol and Middletown, and Levittown ranks third as a census place.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures show 249,187 households, a median home value of $445,700, median household income of $114,764 and an owner-occupied rate of 77.8%. Median gross rent is $1,605. Those numbers explain why many sellers look hard at tax lines on a settlement statement.

  • Main highways include I-95, the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276), US 1, US 202 and US 13.
  • Central and Upper Bucks have kept adding homes, and new construction brings interim assessments.
  • Bensalem, Bristol, Middletown and Northampton townships each had more than 39,000 residents in 2020.

How do you appeal a Bucks County assessment?

You file an appeal form with the Board of Assessment Appeals, 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown, and pay a non-refundable $75.00 filing fee for each parcel. For 2026 the annual appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, counted by postmark or office receipt, and any change from that round takes effect in the 2027 tax year. Check the county's appeal page each summer for the next year's date.

The Board's published rules for residential appeals set out what happens next. Fax filings are rejected, and a form that arrives after the deadline is untimely. The appellant, or an attorney with a signed authorization, has to attend the hearing unless a waiver is signed on the form.

  • Evidence of value can be a Pennsylvania certified appraisal that meets USPAP, or sales within the last 18 months of similar homes in your neighborhood.
  • If you bought within 18 months, add your settlement sheet. It cannot be your only evidence.
  • Notice of the hearing is mailed 20 days ahead, and postponements are not granted.
  • Missing the hearing is treated as abandoning the appeal, and the fee is not returned.
  • Group appeals must be handled by an attorney.

The Board meets the first and third Tuesday of each month at 10 a.m. at the courthouse in Doylestown. Interim appeals, which follow a revision notice, use the deadline printed on that notice and cost the same $75.00.

Does Bucks County offer homestead or other tax relief?

Yes. School districts reduce the assessed value of an owner's primary residence through the homestead exclusion, and farm buildings on at least ten contiguous acres can qualify for a farmstead exclusion. The application for the school tax year beginning July 1, 2027 is due to the Board of Assessment Appeals by March 1, 2027, and it can be downloaded from the county's page if no form came in the mail.

The instructions say you may be asked to prove residency with a driver's license, voter registration or a tax return. A false statement can bring back taxes with interest, a penalty of 10% of the unpaid tax and a fine of up to $2,500. School districts must notify an owner by December 31 each year if an approval is expiring or was denied.

Older and disabled owners can also look at the state Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program. It pays $380 to $1,000 by income, requires household income of $48,110 or less, and the deadline for the 2025 claim year is December 31, 2026. The Department of Revenue's help line is 1-888-222-9190.

What happens when Bucks County taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid taxes become a lien, and after 18 months the Tax Claim Bureau can sell the property. Local tax collectors send delinquent accounts to the Bureau after December 31, and the Bureau mails a Notice of Claim, usually by certified mail the next spring. The county lists the lien as automatic, and it shows in the public record without any filing at the prothonotary.

The upset sale takes place in September of the second year after the first bill. Properties that do not sell move to a continued upset sale and a judicial sale in December. Both run online through GovEase, and the September 15, 2026 upset sale has already taken place. The December 8, 2026 lists are posted on the county's Upset and Judicial Sales page.

  • Partial payments of any amount are accepted without a written plan.
  • An Agreement to Stay Sale sets quarterly payments over 12 months for owners facing a sale.
  • After June 1 of the sale year, payment must be by cashier's check or money order, and 18-month delinquent taxes need certified funds.
  • The Bureau no longer takes cash. It sits at 55 East Court Street, 5th floor, and answers at 215-348-6274 from 8:15 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. on weekdays.

How do property taxes affect closing on a Bucks County sale?

Any county, township or school tax debt is paid out of the seller's proceeds before other debts, so a lien reduces the cash you walk away with. Ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a lien certificate on the county's posted request form before the settlement date. Interim bills matter too, since a recent improvement can add a quarterly charge.

The recorder collects a 2% realty transfer tax at recording, split between the state and the local governments, and the purchase agreement decides who pays it. New owners must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying, under Act 29. A new recorded deed, including a refinance, also ends the homestead exclusion until a new application is filed within 45 days.

Sellers carrying tax debt, an expired homestead or a stalled appeal can sell without fixing each issue first. A buyer who purchases as-is can take over a clean closing with the lien paid from proceeds. Ask the Board and the Bureau for written figures before you accept any offer.

More questions about Bucks County, PA Property Tax Guide

Who do I call about a Bucks County assessment?

Call the Board of Assessment Appeals at 215-348-6219. The office is at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown, and the homestead instructions list office hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., Monday through Friday. Questions about parcel number, municipality or school district go to the same line.

When is the Bucks County homestead exclusion application due?

The application for the school tax year starting July 1, 2027 is due March 1, 2027. File it with the Board of Assessment Appeals. A new recorded deed, including a refinance, requires a new application within 45 days of filing.

What is the filing fee for a Bucks County assessment appeal?

The fee is $75.00 per parcel and it is non-refundable. It applies to annual and interim residential appeals, and the check is payable to the Bucks County Board of Assessment. Do not mail cash.

How long before Bucks County can sell a house for unpaid taxes?

The Tax Claim Bureau can sell a property once a lien stays unpaid for 18 months. Eligible properties go to the upset sale in September of the second year, and unsold ones can move to the December judicial sale. You can stop a sale by paying before the close of business at the courthouse the day before it.

Does Bucks County tax a sale of my house?

Yes, a 2% realty transfer tax is paid when the deed is recorded, with 1% to the state and 1% to the municipality and school district. State and local governments do not say who pays, so the purchase agreement usually divides it. Exemptions exist for some family transfers.

Delaware County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Delaware County, Pennsylvania?

Most of it happens in the Government Center at 201 West Front Street in Media. The Treasurer's self tax collection office on the ground floor takes current year county tax, the Tax Claim Bureau, also on the ground floor, collects back taxes, and the Board of Assessment Appeals hears challenges to assessed value. Treasurer hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays at 610-891-4278.

The county says it has about 200,000 billable properties, and 35% of county tax is paid through mortgage companies and banks. The other 65% is mailed in by owners.

Every parcel has an 11 digit number. The county's own example, 34-00-05432-01, begins with 34 for the township or borough, in that case Nether Providence. Keep that number handy for any call about a bill.

When are Delaware County property taxes due?

County bills are mailed February 1 for the calendar year, and the payment window opens with a 2% discount. The discount ends April 1, face amount is due through June 1, and a 10% penalty applies from then until the end of the year.

Source: the Delaware County Treasurer's current year taxes page. The amount due at face is the assessment multiplied by the county millage rate.

Duplicate bills cost $2.00 per parcel. A paid or unpaid certification for county tax, covering the current year and a three year look back, costs $25.00 and takes a stamped envelope and a check.

How do I appeal a Delaware County assessment?

Annual appeals are due August 1 of the year before the year being appealed. The Board of Assessment Appeals must receive them by hand or have them postmarked by that day, and fax or email filings are not accepted. The Board is at the Government Center, 201 West Front Street, Media, PA 19063.

  • An interim appeal, after a change in assessment, is due within 40 days of the date on the notice.
  • Exemption appeals share the August 1 date.
  • A county processing fee applies to annual appeals: $50 for residential and $100 for commercial or exemption appeals. Interim and reassessment appeals carry no fee.
  • Each parcel needs its own form with an original signature from the owner or a Pennsylvania attorney.

The burden of proof is on the appellant, and the assessment is presumed correct. The Board suggests an appraisal from a licensed Pennsylvania appraiser or proof of a recent sale within a year of the valuation date. Broker price opinions and market analyses are not accepted.

Only the owner or a Pennsylvania attorney can present at the hearing, and an LLC needs an attorney. Skipping the hearing means the appeal is dismissed as abandoned. Notice arrives at least 20 days beforehand.

What happens to unpaid Delaware County taxes?

On March 1 the Tax Claim Bureau starts collecting prior year taxes for the county, the school district and the municipality. Interest runs at 0.75% per month, and a $64 service fee is added, along with costs for notices and documentation before any sale.

Payment is by certified check or money order made out to Tax Claim Bureau. In person, the office also accepts cash and Visa, MasterCard or Discover, with a 3% convenience fee on cards. Payment plans may be offered to qualified owners, and the number for the Bureau is 610-891-4282. Have the 11 digit parcel number ready for any payoff request.

Properties are auctioned each year in the Upset Price Sale. Unsold ones go to a Judicial Sale, held free and clear of liens with court permission, and anything left over lands on a Repository List. The 2026 Upset Price Sale was set for December 10 at 10 a.m., with bidder registration on November 16 and 17, limited to the first 120 bidders. The coordinator can be reached at 610-891-8294.

Is there help for older or low income homeowners in Delaware County?

The county adopted a Real Estate Tax Deferral Program in January 2026 under Act 301 of 1999, effective January 1, 2026. It lets an eligible owner postpone the part of the county bill that comes from millage increases.

  • Household income cannot exceed $48,110, with half of Social Security, SSI and Railroad Retirement Tier 1 excluded from the count.
  • The home must be a house the owner has lived in as a primary residence for the past twelve months, held by a natural person.
  • No delinquent tax can be owed, and the prior year's bill must be paid before December 31.
  • Deferred tax plus other liens and mortgage principal cannot pass 85% of market value, and the mortgage alone cannot pass 70%.

Applications are received from January 1 to October 31 by the Treasurer's office, with proof of income, fire insurance and loan balances. The phone is 610-891-4273.

Deferral is a lien, not forgiveness. The deferred amount comes due when the home is sold, when title passes by will or law, or at the owner's death. A surviving co-owner who stays in the home is not forced to pay.

What should someone selling in Delaware County know?

Deferred tax has to be paid before the house is conveyed, so a seller in the deferral program should ask the Treasurer for the balance well before closing. Market value under that program is the assessed value divided by the State Tax Equalization Board's common level ratio for the county.

The Recorder of Deeds posted a ratio of 1.83 on June 22, 2026, to be used for documents dated July 1, 2026 or later. The same office handles recording in Room 108 of the Government Center, and its records go back to 1789, the year the county was founded.

Chester City stopped requiring its separate property registration form and $10 fee on September 1, 2023. All Chester City properties are subject to a 1.5% transfer tax.

Request a tax certification from the Treasurer or Tax Claim Bureau before listing. The $25 fee covers county, school and municipal delinquent tax.

What does the Delaware County housing picture look like?

The Census Bureau counts 580,937 residents in the July 2025 estimate on just 183.82 square miles, or 3,138 people per square mile, which makes it the densest of the three counties on its comparison table. QuickFacts lists 230,160 housing units, with 69.6% owner occupied.

The median owner occupied home is worth $332,200, median gross rent is $1,372 and median household income is $89,546. The mean commute is 28.1 minutes, the longest of the three counties, and the county recorded 217 building permits in 2025.

More questions about Delaware County, PA Property Tax Guide

When is the Delaware County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 of the year before the year being appealed. Appeals must be hand delivered or postmarked by that date, with an original signature and a $50 residential fee. Fax and email are not accepted.

Does Delaware County give a discount for paying early?

Yes, 2% off if the county bill is paid by April 1, with bills mailed February 1. The face amount is due from April 2 through June 1, and a 10% penalty applies after that until December 31.

What interest does the Tax Claim Bureau charge?

Interest is 0.75% per month on prior year taxes, plus a $64 service fee. Collection of prior year taxes begins March 1. Other costs for notices and documents can be added before any property sale.

Can I defer my Delaware County property tax?

Possibly. The 2026 deferral program covers increases in county tax for owners with household income up to $48,110 who live in the home. The deferred amount is due when the home sells or changes title.

How do I prove my taxes were paid?

Bring documentation to the taxing authority, usually copies of both sides of the cancelled checks or an official receipted bill. Only a municipality or school district can strike a lien through an exoneration letter to the Bureau.

Chester County by the numbers

Who sets and collects property tax in Chester County?

Three layers of government share the bill. The county, one of 14 school districts and, in most places, one of the 73 municipalities each levy a tax, and the County Assessment Office places the value on every parcel that those levies are applied to. Collection of delinquent bills belongs to the Tax Claim Bureau, which operates under the direction of the county commissioners.

State-certified assessors set the values. Whenever an assessment is created or changed, the owner is mailed a Change in Assessment notice, and school districts and municipalities receive the same data so they can bill the new amount. The Assessment Office is at 313 W. Market St., Suite 4202, West Chester, phone 610-344-6105, open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

How is a Chester County tax bill calculated?

The county's formula is assessment multiplied by millage. A mill is one-thousandth of assessed value, so a rate of 5.164 mills equals 0.005164. The county's own example applies that rate to a $100,000 assessment and gets $516.40.

In Chester County the assessment equals 100% of appraised market value as of the base year. The last countywide reassessment took effect for 1998, and the Common Level Ratio exists to account for the gap between assessments and sale prices. The Assessment Office uses the computer-assisted mass appraisal model built before that reassessment when it prices new work, and it cannot apply the Common Level Ratio to its own figures. Millage rates are voted by elected officials who divide the budget by the tax base, so the county, school and municipal rates differ by address. Ask the Assessment Office or your municipality for the rates that apply to your parcel.

When can I appeal my Chester County assessment?

An annual appeal runs from May 1 through the first business day in August, and that window applies to exemption appeals as well. A Board decision on an annual appeal does not change the bill until the following tax year.

Forms must be printed, completed and returned to the office, because faxes and electronic copies are not accepted. The fee is not refunded if you skip the hearing or withdraw. Owners over 60 who cannot pay the $25 can call the Department of Aging at 610-344-6350 about help.

How does an appeal hearing work?

A three-member Board of Assessment Appeals, appointed by the county commissioners for four-year terms, hears each case. Notices go out at least 20 days before the hearing, and hearings take place at the Government Services Center, 601 Westtown Rd., West Goshen Township.

  • Bring recent photographs of the front and rear of the house, taken within the last six months.
  • Bring appraisals or sale records for similar homes nearby.
  • If you cannot attend, send someone with a letter of authorization. Only one of several joint owners needs to appear.

The Board decides a fair market value and then applies the Common Level Ratio. The ratio is set at 30.6% for annual appeals heard in 2026, with Board decisions effective for tax bills issued in 2027. Decisions normally arrive in writing within three to four weeks, though annual appeal results are not mailed until after August 1. A disagreement can go to the Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the Board's notice.

What tax relief is available in Chester County?

Two programs matter most to homeowners. The Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion lowers the assessed value of an owner-occupied home, not a rental or business-only property. Enrollment runs December 15 through the first business day in March, and there is no fee. Approval is not automatic, the exclusion appears as a line on the bill, and an approved owner cannot be made to reapply more than once every three years. Someone who moves must apply again for the new home.

The Clean and Green program under Act 319 has an application window of March 1 through June 1, filed with the Assessment Office. A homeowner who improves a house should also know about interim assessments: a new addition, pool, garage or shed raises the assessment from the first month after completion, and the taxing authorities then bill the increase.

What happens if Chester County property tax goes unpaid?

Taxes are due by December 31 of the year they are levied, and anything unpaid after that is delinquent. Taxing authorities certify unpaid liens to the Tax Claim Bureau by January 15, and return and claim notices are sent by certified mail by July 31. The bureau works under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, Act 542 of 1947.

  • An upset sale is scheduled no earlier than the second Monday in September and no later than September 30 of year two.
  • The sale is advertised at least 30 days ahead, and a second notice goes by first class mail at least 10 days before.
  • The bid price includes current and delinquent taxes, municipal and Commonwealth liens, transfer taxes, recording fees and costs.
  • The court must confirm the sale absolute, a step that takes about four to six months before funds are paid out.
  • An unsold property becomes eligible for a judicial sale, which sells it free and clear of liens and mortgages.

Owners can head off a sale with an agreement requiring at least 25% down and three equal installments, or a deferral of up to twelve months. Both are at the bureau's discretion.

What does Chester County look like for a seller with tax due?

Chester County has about 557,116 residents in 751 square miles around West Chester, with Coatesville the only city. The Census Bureau lists a median owner-occupied value of $485,600 for 2020 to 2024, median household income of $127,208 and owner-occupancy of 75.1%.

With values that high, even a small gap between assessed and market value can make a tax appeal worthwhile. A seller carrying unpaid tax should call the Tax Claim Bureau and the Assessment Office, and ask each for the current balance and any interim assessment pending on the parcel, before agreeing to a closing date.

Chester County's building and permit work can also change the number. Municipal permit offices hand owners a county letter explaining that improvements are assessed, and field visits by a certified Pennsylvania evaluator collect the property data. A buyer's lender will want the billing history clean before closing, so settle any pending interim notice early.

Annual appeals may be filed from May 1 through the first business day in August. Interim appeals after new construction must be filed within 40 days of the Change in Assessment notice.

How much does a Chester County assessment appeal cost?

A residential appeal costs $25, a Clean and Green or Act 515 parcel costs $50, and commercial, industrial and exemption appeals cost $150. The fee is paid at filing and is not refunded.

When does Chester County property tax become delinquent?

Taxes become delinquent after December 31 of the year they are levied. Unpaid taxes can lead to an upset sale held between the second Monday of September and September 30 of the following year.

Apply to the Assessment-Homestead Office between December 15 and the first business day in March. There is no filing fee, and approval is not automatic for owner-occupied homes.

Lancaster County by the numbers

Which Lancaster County offices deal with property tax?

Three county offices cover it, and the first two sit in the Government Center at 150 North Queen Street in Lancaster. The Property Assessment Office sets values, the Treasurer takes county tax payments, and the Tax Claim Bureau, listed under the Treasurer, collects taxes that have gone delinquent.

  • Property Assessment: Suite 310, building entrance on Chestnut Street, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., phone 717-299-8381.
  • Treasurer: Suite 122, phone 717-299-8222, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, with a 9:00 a.m. start on the second Thursday of each month and early or late appointments available.
  • Tax Claim Bureau: delinquent tax reports, sale notices and the repository list are posted on its county page.

The county government, 17 school districts and most of the 60 municipalities levy a property tax, so a Lancaster County tax bill is really several bills. The Assessment Office tracks more than 195,000 parcels for them.

How is a Lancaster County property valued?

By fair market value, which the county defines as the price a willing seller and a willing buyer would agree on in an arm's length sale. A three-member Board of Assessment Appeals hears disputes about it.

The last full reassessment took effect on January 1, 2018, with values pegged to market value as of that date at a 100 percent ratio. A new countywide reassessment sets values for tax year 2027, and the notices went out by mail on June 15, 2026. The county states that a reassessment aims to equalize values and not to raise taxes, since the county, the municipalities and the school districts must adjust their millage so their income does not rise. A taxing body can still raise its rate afterward, as in any other year.

Property records are free to view on the county site, and the county warns owners not to pay for a copy of their record.

What are the property tax appeal deadlines in Lancaster County?

August 1 each year for a standard appeal, or 40 days after a change notice when the Assessment Office changes a value. The county file lists a separate rule for countywide reassessments.

Lancaster County assessment appeal types, Board of Assessment Appeals quick guide
Appeal typeDeadlineFiling fee

An application is filed for each parcel with the Board at the Assessment Office, in person or by mail. The owner of record signs it, or an officer for a company, or a representative under a power of attorney.

Is the 2027 reassessment appeal window still open?

No. The county set the deadline for 2027 reassessment appeals at August 3, 2026, the first business day after August 1, and that date has passed. Its Property Assessment page says the next opportunity for an annual appeal is 2028, with more information due in early 2027.

That does not close every door. A 40-day appeal can still follow a change of assessment notice that the office issues after a property's market value changes.

  • An appeal challenges the assessed value of the property and says nothing about the amount of tax owed.
  • Tax rates differ by municipality and school district, so equal assessments can produce different bills.
  • The county asks owners to consider whether they could sell for the new assessed figure before they file.

What happens at a Lancaster County assessment appeal hearing?

The Board mails the date, time and place to the owner of record, who must tell any representative or witness. Each case takes roughly 5 to 15 minutes, and anyone who testifies signs an oath. The purpose is to determine market value, so the evidence matters more than the argument.

  • A certified appraisal.
  • A recent deed showing the price paid in an arm's length sale.
  • Recent sales of similar properties.
  • A market value analysis prepared by a Realtor.
  • For commercial and industrial property, leases, rent schedules and income and expense reports.

A decision is mailed later. The Board can dismiss an appeal when the owner fails to appear or to produce requested documents, so bring paper, not just an opinion.

Can a homestead enrollment or a land program lower a Lancaster County tax bill?

The Assessment Office keeps homestead enrollment information. It says recent applications may not show on its website yet, and that anyone who has just bought a property should contact the office. Phone before you assume the exclusion is on your record.

Rural parcels sometimes sit in a preferential land program. If yours might, ask the Assessment Office whether the parcel is enrolled and what a sale or a split of the land would change, and get that answer in writing before you sign a contract.

What happens when Lancaster County property taxes go unpaid?

The Tax Claim Bureau steps in. It posts a delinquent tax report on its county page, and that report is marked as uncertified: the total due can change, and interest accrues monthly on the first day of a new month. A seller who owes back taxes should therefore ask for a current payoff figure close to the closing date.

The bureau also runs upset and judicial tax sales, announced in notices on the county site, and keeps a repository list of properties that did not sell. Anyone facing one should call the bureau before the sale date instead of waiting for the notice.

The Real Estate Tax page offers a Request for Waiver of Additional Charges form, which is the route to ask for relief from added penalties. Whether the waiver is granted is the county's decision.

Start with the numbers the county already holds. The Treasurer's page offers a way to pay a county tax bill online, a tax search for Lancaster County properties and a tax certification service. The Tax Claim Bureau, which is part of the Treasurer's office. It posts a delinquent tax report that is not certified, because interest is added on the first day of each month. It also holds the upset and judicial tax sales.

Who handles property tax in Northampton County, Pennsylvania?

The county divides the job in two. The Assessment Office sets and maintains the value of every parcel, while the Revenue and Tax Claim Office bills, collects and chases unpaid taxes. Both sit in the government center at 669 Washington Street in Easton.

Assessment is in Room 2112 on the second floor, phone 610-829-6155. Revenue and Tax Claim answers at 610-829-6186. A third body, the Revenue Appeals Board, hears assessment disputes.

The county has run under a home rule charter since 1978, with an elected executive and a council, and appeal fees are set by council resolution. A seller in Northampton County usually needs two items from these offices: the parcel's current assessment and a tax certification showing what is owed.

How do I appeal a Northampton County assessment?

File with the Revenue Appeals Board by August 1. An annual appeal filed by that date earns a hearing, and any change applies to the following tax year.

  • Residential forms must list the most recent comparable sales. Without them the assessment may stay as it is.

Has the 2026 appeal season ended in Northampton County?

August 1, 2026 has come and gone, and the board's posted hearing dates ran from August 5 through October 29. An owner who missed it waits for the next August 1, unless the county mails a notice of change, which opens a 40-day interim window.

The county posts the Common Level Ratio each July 1, and a seller deciding whether an appeal is worth the effort should ask the Assessment Office for the current figure and the parcel's recent comparable sales.

How does the homestead exclusion work in Northampton County?

It trims the assessed value on which school property tax is computed for a primary residence. Under Act 72 of 2004, school districts draw on state gaming revenue and local income taxes to give every approved homestead the same dollar reduction before the tax is figured.

  • Applications go to the county Assessment Office and are due by March 1.
  • The exclusion applies to one primary residence, so a second home does not qualify.
  • Owners must report a change in use within 45 days, such as turning the house into a rental.
  • A denied application can be appealed within 40 days of the date on the letter.
  • A false application brings back taxes, interest, a 10 percent penalty and possible misdemeanor charges.

Some school boards choose not to adopt the exclusion, so ask your school district what applies. A seller moving out should tell the assessor, since a house that stops being a homestead should not keep the exclusion.

How and where do I pay Northampton County property tax?

The county runs an online portal for current taxes, and its payment page announces that the 2026 real estate tax portal is live. That page lists fees of 3.5 percent for credit cards and $4 for electronic checks under $29,999.

Past-due accounts are handled by phone at 610-829-6186. The county has said it anticipates a separate way to pay balances less than two years behind that are not subject to sale, so ask the Revenue Office which option fits your parcel.

The same page links the tax certification that a closing agent requests. Closing agents commonly ask for it, so order it early instead of waiting for the final week before the closing date.

What happens to unpaid taxes in Northampton County?

They go to the Tax Claim Bureau and can end up at a sale. The county posted a Judicial Sale for May 27, 2026 and an Upset Sale for September 24, 2026, both at 1:00 p.m. in Courtroom 1, and both dates are behind us. The upset sale falls in September each year.

An owner with a lapsed bill should contact the Revenue Office well before September. Ask the Tax Claim Office what clearing the account would take before a sale date. A seller who is behind should tell the title agent at the start.

How can I look up my assessment before listing a house?

The Assessment Office links a public site, ncpub.org, where county assessment data can be reviewed online. Search by address or parcel, then compare the assessed value with recent sales of similar houses on your street.

  • Note the tax map identification: district, map, block and lot. Appeals and the homestead form both ask for it.
  • Check the school district and municipality listed for the parcel, because the homestead application asks for both.
  • Look at the building details, such as rooms, baths, garage and lot size, and report any error to the office.
  • Confirm whether a homestead exclusion is already applied before you sell.

Buyers ask what the tax bill looks like, so having the parcel record ready saves a round of questions. The Assessment Office also offers a change of address form for a tax bill that still goes to an old address.

What is the Northampton County housing picture for sellers?

This Lehigh Valley county spans 377 square miles. Easton is the seat, Bethlehem is the largest city, and the Delaware River marks the eastern border with New Jersey. The county dates to 1752 and long led in steel and cement.

The federal estimate for 2025 is 324,411 residents, up 3.7 percent on the 2020 base. The latest five-year survey puts the median owned home at $308,600, median household income at $89,184 and median gross rent at $1,395. Cities, boroughs and townships all sit inside the same county assessment system, so the parcel record is a better guide to your own tax bill than any county average.

What is the last day to challenge an assessment in Northampton County?

August 1. A yearly appeal reaches the Revenue Appeals Board only if it is filed by then, and any result applies to the next tax year. Interim appeals get 40 days from a notice of change.

What does it cost to file an assessment appeal in Northampton County?

$25 per parcel for a residential appeal and $250 for a commercial or exemption appeal. The money is not refunded, and moving a hearing costs another $25.

Yes, once the residential assessed value reaches $175,000. A state certified appraiser must prepare it, and restricted reports are refused.

By March 1, filed with the county Assessment Office, which sends a written notice if the request is denied.

How long do I have to take a board decision to court in Northampton County?

Thirty days from the mailing date of the board's notice, filed in the Court of Common Pleas. An appellant who abandoned the hearing gives up that right.

Who sets and collects property tax in Luzerne County?

Two layers handle it. The county Assessment Office decides what each parcel is worth, and the municipality and school district where the parcel sits apply their own millage rates to that figure. The county's property tax page says the bill depends on the assessed value from Luzerne County's Assessment Office combined with the mileage rates of your municipality and your school district.

With 76 municipalities in the county and a dozen school districts, two houses with the same assessment can carry different yearly bills. The districts include Wilkes-Barre Area, Hazleton Area, Wyoming Valley West, Pittston Area, Dallas, Crestwood, Greater Nanticoke Area, Hanover Area, Lake-Lehman, Northwest Area, Wyoming Area and Berwick Area. The Assessor's Office is in the Courthouse Annex at 153 North River Street, Wilkes-Barre, and takes calls at 570-825-1540. How do I appeal a Luzerne County assessment?

The county page says it accepts only cash and checks for these payments, and credit cards are refused.

Unpaid taxes can end in a tax sale. Since March 1, 2026 the bureau or its agent collects a $100.00 fee from every buyer at a tax sale, and the county sheriff collects the same amount at mortgage foreclosure sales. The money goes into a county Demolition and Rehabilitation Fund for blighted buildings. Sales to nonprofits, land banks and government bodies are excluded.

  • PIN certification: the Assessor's Office certifies the parcel number on every deed and bills its own fee. The Recorder's schedule says to call 570-825-1525 for the amount.
  • Transfer tax: the county's schedule lists a 2 percent total in most municipalities, 3.5 percent in Wilkes-Barre and Pittston, and 2.5 percent in Kingston Borough. Hazleton's total is 2 percent.

On a $174,000 sale, which is close to the median owner-occupied value, a 2 percent total comes to $3,480, and a Wilkes-Barre sale at 3.5 percent comes to $6,090. The purchase agreement decides who pays it, though both parties are liable to the state, so read that clause before you accept an offer.

The year's real estate tax is also divided between seller and buyer. Ask your closing agent how the split is figured, and check that the bill used is for the right municipality and school district.

What should a seller know about Luzerne County itself?

Luzerne County formed on September 25, 1786 from Northumberland County. It spans 906 square miles in northeastern Pennsylvania and runs on a council-manager home rule form of government. Wilkes-Barre, with 44,328 people in 2020, is the seat. Hazleton follows with 29,963, then Kingston borough with 13,349, Nanticoke with 10,628 and Pittston with 7,591.

The Wyoming Valley, cut by the Susquehanna River, runs through the middle of the county, and mountain ridges rise on each side. Anthracite mining shaped the towns, and the 1930 population of 445,109 has fallen to 325,594 in 2020. Warehousing along Interstates 80 and 81 now employs many residents, with healthcare, universities and power generation behind it.

  • The owner, an authorized representative or a lessee who pays the tax must sign. A corporation signs through an officer.
  • A filing fee is due for every parcel, by check or money order to the Board, and it is never refunded.
  • The Board will not accept or hear an appeal while delinquent taxes remain on the parcel.
  • Only a Pennsylvania attorney may represent an owner before the Board, and the aggrieved party is expected to appear at the hearing.

Settling the balance before a sale keeps the Bureau from moving the parcel toward an upset sale, which is how the Bureau handles unpaid accounts.

Act 29 of 2026, House Bill 858, created a county maintained contact registry for non-owner-occupied property. It took effect September 18, 2026, after being signed July 20, 2026, and owner-occupied principal residences are exempt.

Westmoreland County by the numbers

Which Westmoreland County offices handle property tax?

Three county offices split the job: Tax Assessment sets the value, the Tax Office supports the local collectors, and the Tax Claim Bureau takes over once taxes are delinquent. County offices keep weekday hours from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

The Tax Assessment Office sets, maintains and certifies assessments on all real property in the county, and the county, the school districts and the municipalities all bill from those figures. Staff review every building and demolition permit that municipalities issue, check construction in the field, and mail notices when an assessment changes. The office is at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue, Suite 440, Greensburg, PA 15601.

The Tax Office hands each tax collector the real estate data needed for the year's bills. The Tax Claim Bureau, mandated by Pennsylvania's real estate tax laws, collects delinquent county, municipal and school taxes for all years before the current one, and it holds the tax sales. Its number is 724-830-3428.

Who collects delinquent tax in Westmoreland County, and who does not?

The Tax Claim Bureau does for 65 districts, but not for nine of them. The county lists the exceptions: the City of Greensburg, Hempfield Township, Irwin Borough, the City of Latrobe, North Huntingdon Township, Penn Township, Trafford Borough, Jeannette School District and Monessen School District.

If your house is in one of those places, the back-tax conversation is with the local collector or the municipality, not the county bureau. Before you rely on any payoff figure, confirm which body holds the claim.

  • For a house in the 65 covered districts, call the Tax Claim Bureau at 724-830-3428.
  • For a house in an excepted district, ask the municipal or school district tax office for the balance.
  • Ask for the payoff in writing, with a good-through date, so your closing agent can pay it out of the sale.

How does a Westmoreland County assessment appeal work?

You file with the Board of Assessment Appeals. A taxpayer can appeal a change of assessment within 40 days of the mailing of the notice of change, and anyone can appeal an assessment each year by August 1, with the result taking effect the next tax year.

Forms are available in the Forms section of the county site or at the Tax Assessment office. The county's appeal form states that a signed form has to be back at the office on or before August 1, and faxed or emailed copies are not accepted. The board meets on the second Thursday of each month at 9:00 a.m. in the Tax Assessment Office, fourth floor, Suite 440. Its 2026 meeting dates were January 8, February 12, March 12, April 9, May 14, June 11, July 9, August 13, September 10, October 8, November 12 and December 10.

For a seller, timing matters: an appeal filed by August 1 applies to the following tax year, so ask your closing agent how the current year's bill is being handled.

What happens when delinquent taxes go to a Westmoreland County tax sale?

The county sells the house at an upset sale, then at a judicial sale if it stays unsold. Properties with two or more years of delinquent taxes are the ones that go to the upset sale, and the purpose is to put the property back on the tax rolls.

The 2026 upset sale was held on September 14 at 10:00 a.m. in the Commissioners Meeting Rooms of the Courthouse Annex, and the 2026 judicial sale followed on October 1 at 10:00 a.m. in the first-floor Public Meeting Rooms of the Courthouse. Those dates have passed; the county sets a new schedule each year. Bidders must pre-register at least 10 days before a sale under Act 33, in person for a judicial sale.

In a judicial sale, properties are sold free and clear of taxes, liens, mortgages and judgments, except for liens filed by the U.S. government. The winning bidder pays the bid plus costs, including the $110.25 deed recording fee, 2 percent transfer tax based on assessed value, and a $25.00 deed preparation fee. Unsold property goes to a repository file, and the county says those properties are no longer taxable until someone buys them.

Can a Westmoreland County owner stay out of a tax sale?

Often yes, through a payment agreement, if the delinquency is on a residence. The Tax Claim Bureau accepts agreements from owners with two years of delinquent taxes on their home, from May 1 until the Friday before the annual sale in September. Call 724-830-3428 to find out whether you qualify.

Paying has rules. The bureau takes no personal checks. Accepted payment is cash, money order, cashier's check or certified check, or an online payment. Online fees are 1.00 percent per transaction on personal debit cards and 2.60 percent on personal credit cards. For the 2026 sale, the last day for a card payment was September 4 and the bureau office took payments through September 11, and nothing was taken on the sale day itself.

What is Westmoreland County like for a seller dealing with property tax?

The county covers 1,028 square miles of land near Pittsburgh, and the Census Bureau counts 349,324 residents for 2025, 154,979 households and 78.4 percent owner-occupancy. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $203,500, and owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,452 a month in housing costs.

Greensburg is the seat, and the county's cities are Arnold, Greensburg, Jeannette, Latrobe, Lower Burrell, Monessen and New Kensington. Nineteen school districts, including Greensburg-Salem, Hempfield Area, Norwin and Greater Latrobe, serve the county. The county's Land Bank and Development Authority handle vacant, abandoned and tax-delinquent real estate, buying and repurposing properties to restore tax revenue. The population estimate for 2025 sits 1.5 percent below the 2020 census count.

When is the Westmoreland County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 of each year, for an appeal that takes effect the following tax year. A separate 40-day window runs from the mailing of a notice of change in assessment. File with the Board of Assessment Appeals at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue, Suite 440, Greensburg.

Who do I call about delinquent taxes in Westmoreland County?

Call the Tax Claim Bureau at 724-830-3428. It covers 65 districts, though the City of Greensburg, Hempfield Township and several other places collect their own delinquent taxes.

Can I pay delinquent Westmoreland County taxes by personal check?

No. The bureau accepts cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks, plus online payments. Card payments carry a fee of 1.00 percent for debit and 2.60 percent for credit.

How many years behind triggers a Westmoreland County tax sale?

Two or more years of delinquent taxes. Those properties go to the annual upset sale, then to a judicial sale if unsold. Judicial sale buyers must pre-register at least 10 days ahead, in person.

Does a Westmoreland County tax sale wipe out mortgages?

A judicial sale sells property free and clear of taxes, liens, mortgages and judgments, except U.S. government liens. At an upset sale, the county warns that liens may not be divested, so buyers should order a title search.

Erie County by the numbers

Which Erie County offices handle property tax?

Two county offices matter most to a homeowner: the Assessment Office, which sets the value your tax bill is built on, and the Revenue and Tax Claim Bureau, which collects delinquent taxes. Both work out of Erie County Courthouse, 140 West Sixth Street, Erie, PA 16501. Appeals go to Room 104, and delinquent taxes are paid in Room 110.

The Assessment Office describes its job as assessing all real estate in the county accurately and uniformly while running the various tax programs. The Tax Claim Bureau is one of four divisions of the county Department of Finance. It collects delinquent taxes for the county, for the City of Erie and the other municipalities, and for the school districts, then passes the money out to each of them every month.

Local tax collectors bill current-year taxes. If you need the amount due for the year of a sale, ask the tax collector for your municipality rather than the county.

How do you appeal an Erie County assessment?

File a Notice of Intention to Appeal Property Assessment with the Erie County Board of Appeals, and make sure it arrives between January 1 and August 1. The county's form says appeals are heard from July through October.

  • Use one form for each parcel.
  • Include the county parcel ID, the property location, your own estimate of value and the reason for the appeal.
  • List up to three comparable properties that sold recently or are listed for sale, by county index number, name and address.
  • Pay the non-refundable filing fee with a check made out to County of Erie.

The filing fee is $50.00 for the main parcel, plus $10.00 for each extra parcel that makes up the property as a whole, set by County Council Ordinance No. 157 of 2007. The form warns that comparable assessments are not treated as an indication of fair market value, and an exterior photograph of the property is available at the hearing.

Filing opens your property to revaluation, so the assessment may go down, go up or stay where it is. Think about that risk before you file on a property you plan to sell soon. If a corporation owns the house, the form must be signed by an officer. The county also lists a Catastrophic Loss Appeal form for damage cases.

What exemption and program forms does Erie County offer?

The Assessment Office's Documents and Forms page lists a set of applications that change who is taxed or how much. Some matter to a seller, because a change of owner should be recorded with the county once the deed is done.

  • Application for Homestead and Farmstead Exclusions
  • Application for Exemption From Erie County Real Property Taxes
  • Owner Change Form and Owner Registry Form
  • Clean and Green application, Clean and Green information and the Act 319 Notice of Conveyance
  • Mobile Home Change of Ownership Form
  • Change of Address form

Clean and Green land has its own notice when it is conveyed, so a buyer of a farm parcel should look at that form before closing. The page also posts millage rate charts for every year back to 2011, with a revised chart for 2026. Millage rates differ by municipality and school district, so use the chart that matches the house.

When is the Erie County tax sale?

The 2026 upset sale was set for Monday, September 28, 2026 at 9:00 a.m., held online through GovEase. An upset sale offers parcels whose taxes are at least two years delinquent.

Bidders pay a $60.00 non-refundable registration fee. The minimum bid is about the sum of the delinquent and current taxes plus municipal liens, with a $25 deed preparation fee and a $100 engineering fee on City of Erie properties. A property that does not sell can move to the judicial sale, which is run by a law firm, and the owner of that property may not bid on it.

Can you stop a sale or pay delinquent taxes in Erie County?

Yes. Even after a bid is made at the upset sale, the owner can pay the delinquency before the winning bidder pays the upset price, and the property is treated as if it had never been offered. Once the bidder pays in full by 3:30 p.m. on sale day, there is no redemption period.

Delinquent taxes are paid in Room 110 of the courthouse, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and the office is closed on county holidays. It takes cash, attorney IOLTA checks, money orders, certified checks, business or personal checks and MasterCard or Visa. Online payments carry an extra fee of usually around 3%. Ask the Bureau for a current figure at 814-451-6206 because interest and costs are added from time to time.

A stay of sale agreement works as an installment plan, but it cannot be made online.

  • An owner named on the deed must appear in person with state-issued ID or a passport.
  • The down payment is at least 25% of the most recent two years of delinquent taxes.
  • Any older unpaid taxes must be paid in full.
  • A default bars a new installment agreement for three years.

Can you sell a house in Erie County with property tax still due?

You can, as long as the delinquent balance is paid out of the sale proceeds or before closing. Ask the Tax Claim Bureau for a payoff figure close to the closing date, since interest and costs keep being added, and ask your municipality's tax collector for the amount on the current year's bill.

A house already in the sale process is harder. The owner of a property headed to the judicial or repository sale cannot bid on it, and repository sales carry no right of redemption. If your house is on a published list, talk to the Bureau about a stay of sale before you sign a contract, because that may buy time for a closing.

Title work matters just as much to the buyer. Liens, judgments and rents of record follow a property, which is why tax sale bidders are told to order a title search. A buyer's title agent will do the same on an ordinary sale and will insist on payoff of anything found.

What do Erie County housing numbers look like?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures put the median value of owner-occupied homes in Erie County at $177,000, with 68.1% of homes owner-occupied. There were 110,587 households. Median household income was $63,354, and 14.7% of residents were below the poverty line.

Owners with a mortgage had median monthly costs of $1,393, and those without a mortgage $572, while median gross rent was $904. The county issued 243 building permits in 2025.

When can I file an assessment appeal in Erie County?

Appeal forms are accepted from January 1 through August 1. The county form also says hearings run from July through October.

How much does it cost to appeal an Erie County assessment?

The non-refundable filing fee is $50.00 for the main parcel plus $10.00 for each additional parcel that makes up the property. Checks are made out to County of Erie.

Where do I pay delinquent property taxes in Erie County?

Pay in Room 110 of the Erie County Courthouse, 140 West Sixth Street, Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM. You can also pay online from the parcel's tax page, with an added fee of usually around 3%.

What is a stay of sale agreement in Erie County?

It is an installment plan that keeps a delinquent property out of a tax sale. It needs at least 25% of the last two years of delinquent taxes down, payment of all older taxes, and an owner on the deed appearing in person with photo ID.

Can the owner buy back a house after an Erie County upset sale?

Not after the sale is complete. The owner can pay the delinquency before the winning bidder pays the upset price, but once the bidder pays in full by 3:30 p.m. on sale day there is no period of redemption.
